prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

my old friend I wonder how far north you travel? The road goes west starting two doors up from the Dog’s Bollocks ending at sunset. So many sunsets Facebook and Instagram couldn’t contain them. So many yellow lines, white stripes there’s hardly a Valiant left to defy them. Now the years overtake us. Visits as a boy to Uncle Bruce and Aunty Lindy in their K’Rd council flat led me to the greatness of the great north whipping its dusty tail up to the skyline of Reinga. Yet why do I see your darkness as silence my friend? You’re a sleek black eel pumping blood all the way to Karekare, to Muriwai, to Bethells, to Piha, and our vehicles surf the surges back to K’Rd, back and forth, LOL, rocking up our shock absorbers and surfboards. Keep bringing the waves Great North Road. Keep saving the whales! Keep the toheroas shining tucked away from spades in sandy bolt-holes. Smile in your cars and honk honk honk on the Great North Road.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, Dog, Bollocks

outputs.L1:
My old friend, I wonder how far north you travel.

The road runs west, beginning two doors up from the Dog’s Bollocks and ending at sunset. So many sunsets that Facebook and Instagram could never contain them. So many yellow lines, so many white stripes, that there is hardly a Valiant left to defy them.

Now the years overtake us.

Visits as a boy to Uncle Bruce and Aunty Lindy in their K’Rd council flat first led me to the greatness of the Great North, whipping its dusty tail up to the skyline of Reinga.

Yet why, my friend, do I see your darkness as silence?

You are a sleek black eel, pumping blood all the way to Karekare, to Muriwai, to Bethells, to Piha, while our vehicles surf the surges back to K’Rd, back and forth—LOL—rocking our shock absorbers and surfboards.

Keep bringing the waves, Great North Road. Keep saving the whales. Keep the toheroas shining, tucked away from spades in sandy bolt-holes. Smile in your cars and honk, honk, honk on the Great North Road.
outputs.L2:
Old companion, I ask myself how far into the north you go. Your route turns west, beginning two doors beyond the Dog’s Bollocks and running on until it reaches sunset. There have been more sunsets than Facebook or Instagram could ever hold. There are so many yellow lines and white markings that almost no Valiant remains to challenge them.

Now time is catching up with us. When I was a child, trips to see Uncle Bruce and Aunty Lindy in their council flat on K’Rd first showed me the grandeur of the Great North, flicking its dusty tail toward the horizon at Reinga.

But why, my friend, does your darkness look to me like quietness? You are a smooth black eel, driving blood out toward Karekare, Muriwai, Bethells, and Piha, while our cars ride the rolling motion back to K’Rd and out again, LOL, jolting our shock absorbers and surfboards along the way.

Go on carrying the waves, Great North Road. Go on protecting the whales. Keep the toheroas bright and hidden in their sandy escape holes, safe from spades. Grin from inside your cars and beep, beep, beep along the Great North Road.

The speaker reflects with warmth and nostalgia on an old friend and on the many journeys they once took along the Great North Road. These memories are not simply about travel from one place to another; they are tied to friendship, youth, discovery, and the emotional power of the landscape. The road becomes a pathway into the past, carrying with it the excitement of movement and the deep affection the speaker feels for places once visited and experiences once shared.

The Great North Road is presented as a vast and impressive route, stretching west and north through a series of vivid landscapes. It leads the imagination toward sunsets, open skies, rugged coastlines, and distant beaches. The road seems to move through both physical and emotional territory, passing through scenes filled with light, colour, and energy. Coastal destinations such as Karekare, Muriwai, Bethells, and Piha give the road a strong connection to the wild beauty of the natural world, especially the sea, cliffs, sand, and surf.

The speaker’s sense of the road’s importance began in childhood. Visits to relatives on K’Rd helped shape an early awareness of the Great North Road as something grand and meaningful. From a child’s perspective, the road seemed large, mysterious, and full of possibility. It was not just a street or route, but a symbol of distance, adventure, and connection. These early impressions stayed with the speaker and gave the road a lasting significance.

Throughout the poem, the Great North Road is personified as if it were alive. It is not described as a passive piece of infrastructure, but as a powerful, moving presence that links communities, beaches, memories, and landscapes. It seems to have its own force and rhythm, carrying people toward the west coast and into contact with nature. By giving the road this living quality, the speaker suggests that it has shaped lives and identities, especially through the experiences of travel, surfing, and returning to beloved places.

Overall, the poem celebrates the energy and spirit of the Great North Road. It honours the memories attached to it, the friendships formed along it, and the surf culture connected to the beaches it reaches. At the same time, it expresses a deep respect for the natural world: the sea, the sunsets, the coastline, and the wild places beyond the city. The road becomes a symbol of movement, memory, freedom, and belonging, linking the speaker’s personal history to a broader landscape of beauty and adventure.

At the same time, the poem presents the road as a cultural and historical artery. It links people to one another and to the land, connecting neighbourhoods, coastlines, and histories. The road is not treated as a neutral strip of asphalt, but as a force that carries stories, identities, and relationships across time. Its significance lies in the way it joins the personal with the collective: an individual’s memories become part of a wider cultural map.

In this way, the road becomes a symbol of connection not only between people and places, but also between human activity and the natural world.

It is a route of departure and return, a line connecting city and coast, past and present, people and environment. As both a personal and cultural artery, Great North Road continues to carry the stories of those who travel along it.

**The Dog Bollocks**

In the quiet corner of the village pub, beneath a faded sign that read *The Dog & Bollocks*, locals gathered every evening to share stories, laughter, and the occasional wild rumor. Nobody knew exactly how the place got its strange name, though everyone had a theory.

Some said it was named after a legendary sheepdog who once saved the village from a runaway bull. Others claimed the landlord had chosen the title simply because it made people stop, stare, and walk inside for a drink. Either way, the pub became famous.

Inside, the fire was always warm, the chairs were always mismatched, and the dog—an old terrier named Winston—slept proudly near the bar as if he owned the place. To the regulars, *The Dog & Bollocks* wasn’t just a pub. It was the heart of the village: odd, memorable, and full of character.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse prose poem addressed to Auckland’s Great North Road, weaving in K’Rd, West Coast beaches like Piha and Muriwai, childhood memories, social media sunsets, traffic markings, and a playful environmental note about whales and toheroa.
counterfactuals.output:
Great North Road, you old river of tar, you long black sentence running west from the city’s mouth,

I have known you since childhood, when the back seat was a country of biscuit crumbs and fogged windows, when every set of lights felt like a border crossing, when K’Rd glittered ahead like a loose tooth in the grin of Auckland, all neon, rain, bus stops, music leaking from upstairs rooms, people becoming themselves under awnings.

You carried us past dairies and villas, past ghost signs and new apartments, past the white arrows painted on your skin telling us where to go, as if anyone in this city has ever gone anywhere in a straight line. Your flush medians, your bus lanes, your zebra stripes and yellow no-stopping lines: small commandments laid down by council hands, worn thin by tyres, weather, impatience.

And always, somewhere beyond you, the west was waiting.

Piha with its black sand hot enough to make children dance and curse, Lion Rock crouched like a story older than language. Muriwai with gannets lifting off the cliffs like scraps of paper thrown into the wind. The car smelled of sunscreen, salt, vinyl seats, wet towels; the adults argued softly about the best way home while we slept open-mouthed in the back, our hair full of ocean.

Now the sunsets return to us through phones.

Piha in a square frame. Muriwai in a reel. The sky performing orange and bruised purple for strangers who tap little hearts from bedrooms, buses, lunch breaks, bars on K’Rd where someone is always beautiful and someone is always leaving. Even the sun seems to understand branding, leaning hard into the horizon, giving us content, giving us proof we were briefly alive in good light.

Great North Road, you have watched the city change clothes and names. You have held protest marches, police cars, scooters, prams, students, tradies, aunties with shopping bags, boys trying to look fearless, girls laughing like the future is already theirs. You have heard every language we brought with us and every song we turned up too loud at the lights.

Be gentle with us, old road.

Remind us that the west wind is not an accessory, that the sea is not a backdrop, that whales are not there merely to photobomb our weekend awe, and toheroa are not mythical beach snacks waiting politely under the sand for our nostalgia. Let the dunes keep their secrets. Let the shellfish breathe. Let the whales roll their great punctuation through the gulf and beyond, editing our greed with one slow fin.

Great North Road, I address you as if you can answer,

as if beneath your asphalt you remember the old paths, the wet clay, the birdsong, the feet that came before engines. As if every traffic marking is also a memory: turn here, merge there, give way, slow down, look again.

Take me west, then.

Past K’Rd’s bright bruise, past the childhood house I can no longer enter, past the shops that have become other shops, past the corners where I once waited to be picked up, forgiven, noticed.

Take me toward the beaches where the sand darkens the soles of my feet, where the sunset does not need a caption, where the road finally loosens its grip and the ocean begins speaking in its huge, unfinished voice.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal nostalgic monologue to an old friend who is actually the Great North Road in Auckland, mentioning the Dog’s Bollocks, Uncle Bruce and Aunty Lindy, Reinga, Karekare, Bethells, surfboards, honking cars, and the road as a black eel.
counterfactuals.output:
Old friend,

I know it’s strange to address you like a person, but you were always more than tar and lane markings. You were the Great North Road, yes — but also a spine, a memory, a black eel slipping through Auckland’s wet hands, shining after rain, bending past dairies and villas and traffic lights that blinked like tired gods.

I remember you at dusk, when the cars honked as if trying to wake the dead, or summon them, or complain to the moon. Their headlights moved along your back like little nervous insects. We were young then, or thought we were, carrying surfboards under our arms and salt in our hair though the sea was still miles away, calling from Karekare, from Bethells, from the black sand beaches where the wind could peel your name off your face.

You listened to everything. The wild talk outside the Dog’s Bollocks. The laughter that came loose and rolled into the gutter. The promises made with one hand on a pint and the other on tomorrow’s shoulder. You knew Uncle Bruce and Aunty Lindy before I knew what it meant to leave a place and still be haunted by it. They’d appear in stories like weather: Uncle Bruce with his voice full of gravel and mischief, Aunty Lindy bright as a kitchen window, both of them somehow travelling with us even when we were only standing still.

And further north — always north — there was Reinga, not just a place but a whisper at the end of the country, where spirits lean out over the water and decide whether to vanish. I used to think you knew the way there by instinct. That if I followed your black eel body long enough, past the shops and suburbs, past the honking cars and the petrol stations, past every version of myself I’d abandoned, I might arrive at the place where the oceans argue and the dead step softly into the next room.

Do you remember the surfboards strapped to roofs like prayers? The old wagons groaning westward toward Bethells, toward Karekare, toward that cold green roar? We were always chasing something — waves, girls, weather, the idea that our lives were about to begin. You carried us anyway, patient and slick, your white lines flickering beneath us like bones seen through skin.

Now when I think of you, I don’t see traffic. I see an animal. A black eel, immense and ancient, swimming under the city, under the breweries and bus stops, under the old jokes and the empty lots where our youth used to stand. I see you nosing through the dark, remembering every tyre, every barefoot wanderer, every drunk song, every goodbye swallowed before it could become dramatic.

Old friend, road-friend, eel-friend — you were never only the way to somewhere else. You were the somewhere. You were the long sentence we were living inside. And even now, when I am far from your bends and fumes and rain-polished skin, I can feel you moving beneath me, carrying Uncle Bruce’s laugh, Aunty Lindy’s light, the Dog’s Bollocks at closing time, the black sand of Karekare, the salt-blown hush of Bethells, and the last northern breath of Reinga.

Keep swimming, old mate.

I’m still following.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a contemporary New Zealand road poem in one paragraph, with a mix of humour and lyricism, about travelling west and north from Karangahape Road along Great North Road to the beaches?
counterfactuals.output: Leaving Karangahape Road with a coffee hot enough to qualify as a minor volcano and a playlist arguing with the indicators, we roll west and north onto Great North Road, past dairies glowing like small secular chapels, past villas leaning into their own histories, past the bus stops where everyone looks as if they’ve just remembered a better life in Ōpononi; the city loosens its belt at Grey Lynn, then Avondale offers horses, markets, and the philosophical certainty of a pie in a paper bag, and somewhere beyond the roundabouts and roadworks the light begins to change, goes green-gold and salt-minded, pulling us through Titirangi’s bushy eyebrows, the ranges rising like old aunties with opinions, until the tyres start speaking fluent gravel and the wind arrives wearing jandals; at Piha the surf throws itself at the land like a dramatic ex, Lion Rock sits there unimpressed, and we stand with sand in our shoes and the whole Tasman Sea shouting kia ora, while up toward Muriwai the gannets stitch white commas into the cliff air, and even the car, bug-splattered and smug, seems to understand we have travelled not far in kilometres but properly, from neon and noodles to flax, foam, and the big blue mouth of the west, where the horizon keeps promising north, north, keep going.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental prose poem that personifies Great North Road as a living creature, includes Auckland landmarks, west coast surf culture, old family visits in a council flat, and ends with an upbeat chant-like celebration of the road.
counterfactuals.output:
Great North Road wakes before the buses,  
spine slick with rain, ribs humming under streetlights,  
a long old taniwha of tar and grit  
stretching from the city’s glass teeth  
past shopfronts blinking awake in Grey Lynn,  
past villa verandahs and dairies with their lolly jars,  
past the ghost-breath of tramlines,  
past the Karangahape night still glittering in its throat.

It sniffs the harbour wind.  
It has heard the Sky Tower mutter weather to the clouds.  
It has watched Maungawhau/Eden rise and brood,  
green-shouldered, crater-hearted,  
while traffic beads like sweat along its back.

In the old days we visited Auntie in the council flat,  
up the stairs that smelt of boiled cabbage, damp carpet,  
Lux soap, cigarettes, and someone’s dinner singing onions.  
She kept the TV talking in the corner,  
tea bags drying in a saucer for one more cup,  
biscuits in a tin that clicked like a secret.  
Through the window the road shifted and breathed,  
a huge animal waiting below,  
carrying uncles in Falcons, cousins in bare feet,  
Mum with her handbag clamped tight as a prayer.

Great North Road remembered us.  
It licked oil from its paws.  
It wore bus stops like earrings.  
It swallowed coins, brake squeal, school bells,  
the blue uniforms of kids running late,  
the weekend roar toward the wild west—

Piha, Karekare, Muriwai, Bethells—  
names flung like black sand into the mouth of morning.  
Boards strapped to roofs. Wax under fingernails.  
Wetsuits steaming in the boot.  
Somebody’s brother talking big about the sets,  
somebody’s cousin reading the tide like scripture.  
The road flexed its shoulders and carried them out,  
through suburbs thinning to bush,  
through the green hush before the sea appears,  
until the coast stood up in its black iron mood  
and surfers ran laughing into the cold foam,  
salt-bright, fearless, young for a minute.

At night Great North Road curls around memory.  
Neon pools in its eyes.  
Rain tattoos its hide.  
It dreams in petrol, pōhutukawa, pie-shop steam,  
in the soft thump of bass from a passing car,  
in aunties waving from balconies,  
in gulls above the landfill,  
in city lights scattered like loose change behind us.

O old road, patched road, hungry road, home road—  
you carry our errands and our escapes,  
our funerals, first jobs, fish-and-chip packets,  
our surfboards, prams, hangovers, hymns.  
You are not just a road.  
You are a long breath we keep taking.

So sing it up—

Great North, roll on!  
Great North, shine on!  
Tar heart, strong heart, carry us on!  
From Queen Street glow to west coast foam—  
Great North Road, road-home, road-home!  
Beat of the tyres, clap of the rain,  
Great North Road, we ride you again!  
Hey! Haere! Roll on, roll on!  
Great North Road, forever strong!
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rambling poetic tribute to Great North Road, starting “my old friend,” with references to sunsets, yellow lines and white stripes, Facebook and Instagram, whales, toheroas, cars, surfboards, and “honk honk honk.”
counterfactuals.output:
my old friend, Great North Road,  
you long-backed creature of tar and memory,  
you whale of the suburbs rolling quietly through the dusk,  
carrying cars, surfboards, secrets, shopping bags,  
the last heat of the day,  
the first sigh of the night,  
and all of us, somehow,  
somewhere between home and leaving.

I have seen sunsets spill across you  
like orange paint from a careless god,  
gold running down windscreens,  
pink caught in the power lines,  
clouds bruised purple above the shops,  
and you just keep going,  
yellow lines humming at your edges,  
white stripes flashing like old piano keys  
under tyres, under feet, under the hurry  
of people who forgot to look up.

Great North Road,  
you have heard everything —  
the whisper of rain in the gutters,  
the grumble of buses,  
the laugh from an open window,  
the impatient chorus of  
honk honk honk,  
as if the whole city were a flock of geese  
late for dinner.

You have watched us grow vain and glowing,  
posting our little lives to Facebook and Instagram,  
sunset behind us, coffee beside us,  
captioned with hearts and fire emojis,  
while you, old friend,  
wear no filter,  
need no likes,  
ask no one to follow,  
though everyone does.

And somewhere in your long dreaming  
there is the sea —  
whales rising dark and holy beyond the harbour,  
toheroas hidden in the sand like small old songs,  
salt on the wind,  
surfboards strapped to roofs,  
summer boys and winter women  
chasing waves, chasing weekends,  
chasing that impossible blue  
at the end of the road.

You are not beautiful in the easy way,  
not all polished glass and postcard grace.  
You are patched, painted, crowded, loud.  
You are takeaway steam, petrol shine,  
rainbow oil in a puddle,  
a dog barking behind a fence,  
a cyclist leaning hard into the climb,  
a grandmother waiting at the crossing  
beside the white stripes,  
trusting the world to stop for a moment.

my old friend, Great North Road,  
keep your yellow lines bright,  
keep your white stripes brave,  
keep carrying us through sunsets and traffic,  
through honk honk honk and silence,  
through the years we photograph  
and the years we simply survive.  
May the cars pass kindly over you,  
may the surfboards point seaward,  
may the whales keep singing offshore,  
may the toheroas sleep deep in the sand,  
and may we remember, now and then,  
to thank the road beneath us  
for knowing the way.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
